newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Fears grow that EMU row may snag EU treaty reforms.
newsitem.headline: Fears grow that EMU row may snag EU treaty reforms.

text.p: Carefully laid plans to keep economic and monetary union (EMU) from gatecrashing next week's European Union summit in Amsterdam were unravelling on Tuesday in the wake of French doubts over the bloc's stability pact.
The two-day Amsterdam meeting was supposed to be a largely EMU-free zone, allowing EU leaders to focus on revising the Maastricht Treaty to prepare the bloc for enlargement.
Until Monday, most observers had expected the summit to approve the stability pact which was agreed after hard-fought negotiations between France and Germany last December.
But the arrival of France's socialist government has changed all that, prompting fears EMU and the ongoing inter-governmental conference (IGC) are on a collision course at Amsterdam.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his EU partners in Luxembourg on Monday that Paris needed time to study the stability pact, an integral part of monetary union aimed at keeping budget deficits tight after the euro-launch.
The bloc's executive Commission is now rushing to find a way to paper over the cracks and rescue the summit from degenerating into a Franco-German row over the future single currency.
Germany, which thought up the stability pact, wants the euro to be as strong as the mark and has called for tough budgetary discipline and strict adherence to EMU criteria.

French premier Lionel Jospin, who swept to power on a wave of voter opposition to austerity measures designed to see France qualify for EMU, insists more emphasis should be put on job creation and coordinating economic policies within a euro zone.
In addition, Germany wants an independent European Central Bank to set the bloc's monetary policy, while France has argued for a political counter-balance providing "economic government".

European Commission President Jacques Santer will visit Jospin and President Jacques Chirac in Paris on Thursday to try to resolve France's concerns that the stability pact should do more for employment.

"A text will be prepared for Amsterdam," outgoing Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn said late on Monday, but other sources said it was unlikely any breakthrough could be made in time for the pact to be signed at Amsterdam.
Leaders of France and Germany, the bloc's twin powerhouse in political and economic terms, are due to meet in Poitiers in western France on Friday.
The current Dutch EU presidency said there were no plans yet to hold special meetings of the 15-member bloc's foreign or finance ministers ahead of Monday's Amsterdam summit.
"We don't exclude anything, but at the moment we don't foresee anything like that," a foreign ministry spokeswoman said. No one at the finance ministry was immediately available for comment.

Financial markets have been rocked by France's doubts over the pact and, despite official protestations that EMU remains on track for a January 1, 1999 launch, there are growing concerns that monetary union may have to be delayed.
Reaffirming France's commitment to seeing EMU start on time, Strauss-Kahn said he did not want to renegotiate the pact but was unhappy with the current deal, agreed by his predecessor.

While the bloc had hoped to keep EMU at bay during the summit, some EU officials say monetary union and the IGC had been linked all along because part of the treaty negotiations include debate on a so-called Employment Chapter to make job creation a formal EU priority.
EU leaders are also expected to agree on final designs for the new euro coins due to enter circulation by 2002.

European monetary affairs commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy insisted on Tuesday that EU leaders had to agree on the single currency at Amsterdam if the ambitious project was to retain its credibility with financial markets.
"Amsterdam can be a success, must be a success, will be a success, because no one...will put the brakes on the euro," he told the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

Markets will be looking for signals that the EMU framework -- legal texts on the stability pact, a post-euro Exchange Rate Mechanism and the status of the euro -- is in place on schedule by the end of this month.
The IGC talks must also be wrapped up by July to trigger accession negotiations early next year with eastern Europe's former communist states.
